why: Kc8 walks the king into a forced queen mate; check the opponent's mating nets before stepping the king.
Be5 lets f4 hit the bishop with tempo and the b2 pawn falls; Qd6 wins it instead.
Nc3 is kicked by d4; taking on d5 first keeps the initiative.
Grabbing c2 leaves the king on c8 exposed to Bd7+ and Rd8+ instead of consolidating.
Bd7 is passive; a5 attacks the b4 pawn and challenges White's queenside.
Retaking on d4 ignores the loose g5 pawn that Bd3 first would win.
Rd4 ignores the threat on the d3 rook line and Bf5 and Bxc2 gain tempi; Rd2 answers it.
d5 pushes into a square attacked more than defended; take the loose c4 pawn instead.
e6 ignores Black's g5 and d3 ideas; d3 first deals with the pawn pressure.
Castling queenside takes the rook off e8, leaving the e7 knight undefended.
Nc6 allows d5 and Rc8+ with the king boxed on the back rank; Kf8 gives it room.
Nb4 lets d4 attack the knight and the c5 bishop together.
Kf6 ignores the rook on c6 hitting a6 and the a-pawn falls; Re8 keeps the rook active.
Ke7 leaves the king in the centre facing checks and rook invasion; Kd7 is safer.
Nf4 leaves d4 hanging with check on b6 and ignores the Be3+ threat; f4 covers it.
